quote: und auch fragen ob man nicht auch die Glieder $\frac{1}{(x-\alpha)^2}$ unterdrücken will und blos $\frac{1}{(x-\alpha)^3}$ übrig behalten will.
english: And one can also ask whether one might not also suppress the terms $\frac{1}{(x-\alpha)^2}$ and keep only $\frac{1}{(x-\alpha)^3}$.
topic: Hilbert extends an idea from spherical functions (Kugelfunktionen) to algebraic functions, Riemann surfaces, automorphic functions and the Lamé differential equation, and examines the conformal map given by the quotient of two integrals, with a footnote on the inverse of an integral involving $P_n$.

triage.modern_statement: This is my reading of the question, not something the sources state. In the classical case of spherical functions, the second solution of the Legendre equation is Q_n = P_n · ∫ dx / ((1−x²) P_n(x)²). When you expand that integrand into partial fractions at the zeros α of P_n, the simple-pole terms 1/(x−α) have zero residue. So the integral has no logarithms there, and only the terms 1/(x−α)² remain. That vanishing-residue condition is the same as Stieltjes' electrostatic equilibrium condition for the zeros of Heine–Stieltjes/Lamé polynomials. Hilbert seems to ask whether one can go one order higher: find polynomials (or Lamé-type or automorphic analogues) P whose zeros make both the 1/(x−α) and the 1/(x−α)² terms vanish in a suitable integrand built from P (for example, ∫ dx / P³ times a weight), so that only third-order poles 1/(x−α)³ are left. Then the integral, and the conformal map given by the quotient of two integrals, has a prescribed branching type at the zeros.
triage.answered_by: No specific later answer was found. A related but different line of work: Stieltjes (1885) gave the electrostatic interpretation of zeros of Lamé/Heine–Stieltjes polynomials, and Shapiro and coauthors (2008 onward) developed Heine–Stieltjes theory for higher-order differential operators. Neither is shown to answer Hilbert's question about removing the double-pole terms.

evidence.claim: Stieltjes studied the generalized Lamé differential equation in algebraic form and interpreted the zeros of its polynomial solutions as positions of electrostatic equilibrium. This is the classical setting in which the 1/(x−α) residue terms vanish.
Stieltjes gave an electrostatic-equilibrium interpretation of the zeros of Jacobi, Laguerre and Hermite polynomials (including Legendre).

Modern work extends Heine–Stieltjes theory to univariate linear differential operators of higher order. This is a related generalization, but it does not obviously address Hilbert's question about suppressing the 1/(x−α)² terms.

triage.why: The note is a short follow-up question and its exact setup depends on the rest of page [44]. I reconstructed it as a higher-order version of the Legendre/Lamé condition that the residues vanish, but that is an interpretation. Searching found the classical Stieltjes/Heine–Stieltjes theory and modern higher-order Heine–Stieltjes work, which are related. I found no source that poses or answers the question of removing both the simple-pole and double-pole terms. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. I can't confirm whether it was solved or is still open, so the verdict is 'possibly_unexplored' with low confidence.
